media_work.title: Picking Cotton: Our Memoir of Injustice and Redemption
media_work.creator_name: Jennifer Thompson-Cannino, Ronald Cotton, with Erin Torneo
media_work.focus_or_theme: Eyewitness misidentification, wrongful conviction, forgiveness, and reconciliation
media_work.key_statistics: New York Times Bestseller, being adapted into a major motion picture

key_quotes_raw: "Jennifer Thompson was raped at knifepoint by a man who broke into her apartment while she slept. Wearing only a blanket, she escaped and told police she was certain she could identify the man who had been inches from her face."

"Jennifer's misidentification of Ronald serves as a striking example of what is known technically as 'unconscious transference.' For Jennifer, this chain began when she attempted to translate her memories from that dark, traumatic summer night into concrete, usable information by working with police to assemble a composite sketch."

"Many variables can contribute to mistaken identification—for example, a person is more likely to make a mistake when trying to identify someone from a different race than their own—and the complexity of the issue is part of the reason it is the leading factor in wrongful convictions."
systemic_issues_raw: Over-reliance on eyewitness testimony in criminal trials
Lack of proper safeguards in photographic and in-person lineups
Reinforcement of identifications by police and prosecutors
Psychological factors affecting memory and recall during traumatic events
policy_recommendations_raw: Recording of confidence statements at the time of initial identification
Proper training for law enforcement on memory and identification issues
Greater scrutiny of eyewitness testimony in court proceedings
additional_resources_raw: The book's website (pickingcottonbook.com) contains case files, photos, and documents
The Innocence Project website provides additional information on eyewitness misidentification
The book is being adapted into a major motion picture

research_notes_other.this_book_is_particularly_valuable_for_o:
1. Provides a unique dual perspective from both the wrongfully convicted person and the victim/witness who misidentified him
2. Focuses on eyewitness misidentification, the leading cause of wrongful convictions
3. Explores the psychological aspects of memory and identification
4. Documents the process of exoneration through DNA evidence
5. Offers a powerful story of reconciliation and forgiveness between victim and wrongfully convicted person
6. Has received widespread recognition (New York Times Bestseller) and is being adapted into a film, indicating its cultural impact
The book stands out from others in our research as it presents both sides of a wrongful conviction case, offering insights into the experiences of both the person wrongfully convicted and the victim whose testimony contributed to that conviction. It also explores the aftermath of exoneration and the unique relationship that developed between Thompson and Cotton, providing a perspective on healing and reconciliation that is rare in literature on wrongful convictions.

media_item.item_title: Book Content: Picking Cotton: Our Memoir of Injustice and Redemption
media_item.focus_or_theme: Eyewitness misidentification, wrongful conviction, forgiveness, and reconciliation
media_item.summary_notes: This memoir offers a dual perspective on a wrongful conviction case, detailing the experience of both the wrongfully convicted individual, Ronald Cotton, and the victim who misidentified him, Jennifer Thompson-Cannino. It explores the impact of eyewitness misidentification, the exoneration process through DNA evidence, and the subsequent reconciliation between the two individuals.  The book highlights systemic issues within the criminal justice system and offers policy recommendations for reform.
media_item.case_details_raw: Ronald Cotton was wrongfully convicted of the rape of Jennifer Thompson in Burlington, North Carolina, in 1985.  His conviction was based largely on Thompson's eyewitness identification, despite the fact that she later identified another man as her assailant.   Cotton served 11 years of a life plus 54-year sentence before DNA evidence exonerated him in 1995. The book details the challenges of cross-racial identification and flawed lineup procedures that contributed to the misidentification.

featured_individuals.crime_convicted_of: Rape of Jennifer Thompson and another woman
contributing_factors_raw: "Unconscious transference" where the composite sketch influenced later identification
Reinforcement of identification by police and court proceedings
